about: Twelve laws on the trader’s two helpers: the merchant’s agent, who carries his silver and goods out on the road, and the tavern-keeper, who sells beer on credit. The first of them, the end of the law on the agent’s account, is the first thing the stele gives again after the erased columns (the beginning of that law was read from the Nippur tablet in the part before): the agent writes out the interest on the silver he took and pays his merchant (§100); if he found no profit he doubles it (§101), if he met a loss he returns the capital (§102), and if an enemy robs him on the road he swears an oath and goes free (§103). When goods are handed over for trading the agent must take a sealed receipt for what he gives back, and silver without one is not entered in the account (§104–105). An agent who takes silver and then disowns his merchant pays three times over; a merchant who disowns his agent pays six times (§106–107). The tavern-keeper laws follow: grain refused and silver taken by the heavy weight, and the beer-rate cut below the grain-rate, is punished by drowning (§108); criminals gathering in her house and not brought to the palace, by death (§109); a priestess who does not live in the cloister and opens or enters a tavern is burned (§110); beer lent on credit is repaid in grain at harvest (§111). Signs: where a Sumerogram is a group, Harper’s glossary gave its signs and the plates were matched to them; the notes say where that rests on his word.

sentences.i: The interest on the silver, as much as he took, he shall write out; and they shall count his days, and he shall pay his merchant.
sentences.n: This is the end of a law whose beginning stood in the erased columns (the previous part gives it from the Nippur tablet: a merchant gives silver to his agent to trade with and sends him on a journey). The stele picks it up in the middle, so the subject, the agent, is not written here. What you need to read it: ṣibāt kaspim, “the interest of the silver” (ṣibtum), with mala ilqû, “as much as he took” — mala, “as much as”, starts a relative clause and its verb ends in the subjunctive -u. isaddarma is the verb sadārum, “to set in a row, put in order”, so “to write out (an account)”; Harper lists the same forms under šaṭāru, “to write”, and the sense is the same. imannûma is manûm, “to count”, in the 3rd person plural: an impersonal “they shall count”, as we would say “his days shall be counted” — probably the days the silver was out, since interest runs by the day. Last, the merchant is paid: tamkāršu ippal, “he shall pay his merchant” (apālum, “to answer, pay”). Each -ma joins one step of the reckoning to the next (the “and” chain). ūmīšu is written UD-mi-šu: the day-sign UD, a phonetic -mi and -šu, “his”.

sentences.i: If, where he went, he saw no profit, he shall double the silver he took, and the agent shall give it to the merchant.
sentences.n: The agent is the šamallûm, the merchant’s travelling trader. His name is a Sumerogram, three signs that Harper’s glossary gives as SA.GAN.LAL (the modern ŠAMAN₂.LÁ): I write them ŠÀ.GAN₂.LÁ and they recur all through the part. On the plate the first two signs are drawn as one fused group, followed by a separate LÁ (a vertical wedge with a horizontal at its head: Harper’s List of Signs no. 181); Harper’s list shows the same fused group under no. 161 as šamallu. Splitting it into ŠÀ + GAN₂ is a convention, not something the fused shape proves. A šumma-clause with ašar, “where”: ašar illiku, “where he went” (the verb takes -u after ašar), then nēmelam lā ītamar, “he did not see profit”; in a šumma-clause the negative is lā (the main-clause “shall not” is ul, as in §105). kaspam ilqû is a relative clause with no ša: “the silver (that) he took”. uštašannâma is uncertain: šanûm is “to repeat, do twice”, and this Š-stem perfect is read “he shall double (it)”, which fits the penalty; Harper’s glossary lists it as a Š-stem perfect of šanû, “to duplicate, to double”, and finds the same form again in cols. XX, XXI and XXVI; the Nippur tablet, in the part before, has it too, but uncertainly. The ruling ends with ana tamkārim inaddin, “to the merchant he shall give”: inaddin is the present of nadānum, “to give”, used for “shall”.

sentences.n: The law goes on in the next unit: this is only the first half of its “if” (the -ma at the end of ittadinma, “he has given, and”, hands the sentence on). The new word is tadmiqtum, Harper’s tadmiqtu, “favor”: it comes from damāqum, “to be good”, and means “a doing of good, a kindness”. Silver given ana tadmiqtim, “for a kindness”, looks like an advance made on trust, but the commercial sense is a guess from the words. ittadin is the perfect of nadānum, “to give”, the tense for something already done (the present inaddin of §101 is “he shall give”). kaspam is the usual KÙ.BABBAR, with no ending written.

sentences.i: and where he went he met a loss, he shall give the merchant back the capital of the silver.
sentences.n: The rest of §102. The two halves of §101 and §102 mirror each other: there “he saw no profit” (nēmelam lā ītamar), here “he saw a loss” (bitiqtam ītamar), the verb amārum, “to see”, meaning “to meet with”. bitiqtum is “loss, damage” (Harper bitiqtu, “loss, reverse”). The ruling is that he returns only the capital: qaqqad kaspim, “the head of the silver”, is the principal as against the interest — the stele spells it ga-ga-ad, with g, for the word the code elsewhere writes SAG.DU. utâr is the present of târum in the D-stem, “he shall hand back”.

sentences.n: ilqēma is leqûm in the preterite, “he took”, plus -ma (the perfect is ilteqe, as in §105). sentences.n: The merchant brings proof; the agent pays threefold. tamkārum šū is “that merchant” (šū, “he, that”, set after the noun). ina maḫar ilim u šībī, “before the god and the witnesses” (maḫar, “in the presence of”; šībī, genitive plural of šībum, “witness”). ina kaspim leqîm is ina with the infinitive of leqûm: “in the taking of the silver”, that is, “for having taken it”. ukānma is the D-stem of kânum, “to establish; to convict”, the verb of proof: ukān šamallâm, “he shall convict the agent”. a-du 3-šu is the code’s multiplier: adi, “up to”, with a numeral and -šu, “up to threefold”, that is “three times (as much)”. sentences.n: The ruling, the mirror of §106: now the agent proves his case, and the merchant pays sixfold, twice the agent’s penalty. The wording repeats §106, the roles swapped: ina maḫar ilim u šībī … ukānma, a-du 6-šu … inaddin. The new words: aššum, “because (of)”, followed by the clause tamkārum aššum šamallîšu ikkiru, “the merchant, because he denied his agent” — ikkiru is the preterite of nakārum with the subjunctive -u that every verb takes after aššum. šamallīšu is the Sumerogram ŠÀ.GAN₂.LÁ with -šu, “his”. mimma ša ilqû is “whatever he took”: here the subject of ilqû is the merchant, who took the agent’s returned goods. Harper’s ša-mallî-šu, split at the line end, is one word.

sentences.i: If a tavern-keeper did not receive grain as the price of beer, but received silver by the heavy weight,
sentences.n: The tavern-keeper laws begin (§108–111); the tavern-keeper is the woman who brews and sells beer and wine. Her name is the Sumerogram ŠAL.GEŠ.TIN.NA, “woman” + “wine”: Harper gives only the signs, and I read it sābītum (“tavern-keeper”) as the modern editors do. Its signs, from Harper’s list, are SAL, GEŠ (his sign 94, the one the code also uses for “beer” and for syllable bi), TIN (no. 178) and NA. The first rule of the trade is the standard of payment: ana šīm šikarim šeʾam lā imtaḫar, “for the price of beer she did not accept grain” — šīm, “the price”, is the sign ŠÁM (Harper’s no. 83, šîmu); šikarim, “of beer”, is KAŠ (the sign 94 again; Harper’s šikaru). imtaḫar is the perfect of maḫārum, “to receive” (Harper: “to receive”; the same verb meant “to face” in the other parts). ina abnim rabîtim is “by the large stone”: NA₄ (Harper’s abnu) is the stone used as a weight, so a heavy standard — she takes silver weighed on a heavier standard than the usual one (the sense is from the context). rabîtim is the feminine of rabûm, “great”, with the stone treated as feminine.

The verbs are in the plural with no subject: “they” are the judges.

sentences.i: If a priestess who does not live in the cloister
sentences.n: The “if” of §110 begins with two uncertain items. The first word is three signs, ŠAL.NIN.AN: Harper’s transliteration prints aššatum NIN.AN, “a woman, a NIN.AN”, and his index lists the group as SAL.NIN.AN; he gives it no reading, and his translation calls her “a priestess”. NIN.AN is a priestly title (“lady of the god”; the later writing is NIN.DINGIR). Harper’s own text has it standing alone at XXI 26 and, at XXX 61 and XXXI 20, first in a list of several kinds of woman, so it names a class of its own and is not simply the nadītum. Later editions read it ugbabtum, and I follow that; the ŠAL before it is perhaps only the sign that marks a woman’s title. The reading is uncertain: it rests on the sign group and the context, not on a spelled word. The second is MAL.GE.A: Harper leaves it unread (his List of Signs no. 101 shows the group, and GE is his no. 122); I take it as gagûm, the cloister, the walled house in which these priestesses lived, so ša ina gagîm lā wašbat is “who does not live in the cloister” (wašbat is the stative of wašābum, “to live”). The cloister reading is also uncertain.

sentences.i: If a tavern-keeper gave sixty qa of U.SA.KA.NI beer on credit, at harvest she shall take fifty qa of grain.
sentences.n: The last law of the part: beer lent against the harvest. The qa is the measure of capacity (about a litre); Harper writes “LX QA” and “L QA”. On the plate the sixty is the single tall vertical wedge (Harper’s list of numerals gives the same wedge as 60) and no separate sign for qa follows it: the measure is understood, so “sixty qa” is Harper’s expansion. The fifty is a single ligature, the numeral and the measure fused (the sign Unicode calls 5 BAN₂, “five times ten qa”; Harper’s list of numerals shows “50 KA” fused in the same way), so “fifty qa” is read from the one sign. U.SA.KA.NI is four signs that Harper leaves unread (on the plate a grid-like sign, SA, KA and NI); it must name a kind of beer, but I do not know the word, so it is said usakani and not translated. Line 49 has five signs on the plate, matching the words: the fused 50-qa sign, ŠE, i, li, qi. a-na di-ib-tim is ana dibtim, “on credit (?)” — Harper’s own glossary has diptu, “credit(?)”, with a question mark. ina ebūrim, “at harvest” (BURU₁₄, drawn as two pieces, as in Harper’s list no. 19, ebûru; as in §47). The law fixes the repayment: grain, at the harvest, and fifty qa for the sixty of beer.

glossary.-ma: and (clause-chaining particle); also “it is X that…”
glossary.-ši: her / it (3rd-person feminine singular suffix, on a verb): ukannūšima “they shall convict her”, inaddûši “they shall throw her”, iqallûši “they shall burn her”
glossary.-šu: his / him · -šum “to him, for him” (dative): išakkanūšum, innadnušum · after a dental the suffix is assimilated and spelled with z: …ssu (ṣibat-zu, ṣibassu “its interest”, written after a broken sign); with a noun: ṣibtišu “its interest”, qātīšu “his hand”, damqaršu “his merchant”; tu-šu, te-šu in broken forms
glossary.-šum: to him, for him (dative suffix -šum, on a verb): ibaššišum “there is to him”, iqbišum “he said to him”, inaddiššum “he shall give him”
glossary.3-šu: threefold — the numeral 3 with -šu: adu 3-šu (a-du 3-šu) “three times over” (spoken form reconstructed)
glossary.5 BAN₂: fifty qa — the numeral 50 fused with the measure sign (five ban₂ of ten qa each; Harper “L QA”), one ligature on the stone; said ḫamšā qû (spoken form reconstructed). The qa is a measure of capacity
glossary.6-šu: sixfold — the numeral 6 with -šu: adu 6-šu (a-du 6-šu) “six times over” (spoken form reconstructed)
glossary.60: sixty — a single vertical wedge (the sexagesimal “one” of the next order); said šūši (?) “sixty” · here before KAŠ “beer”, with the measure (qa) understood and not written: šūši šikarim “sixty (qa) of beer”; spoken form reconstructed
glossary.abnum: stone; a stone used as a weight (written NA₄; Harper abnu): ina abnim rabîtim “by the large stone”
glossary.adi: up to, times: adi 12-šu “twelvefold” · as a conjunction, “as long as”, with the subjunctive: adi kirâm ṣabtu “as long as he holds the orchard” · adu 3-šu, adu 6-šu “three times, six times (as much)” — the multiplier, spelled a-du (Harper’s variant of adi; the plate has the sign DU)
glossary.alākum: to go: illak “he shall go” · illiku “(where) he went” (preterite, subjunctive -u, after a restored ašar), in the agent law · alākišu (a-la-ki-šu) “his going” (infinitive with -šu): ina alākišu “in his going”
glossary.amārum: to see, examine: immarūma “they shall examine” · ītamar “he has seen” (perfect, singular) · ītamar (i-ta-mar, perfect) “he saw”: lā ītamar “he did not see”; of a loss, “he met with”: bitiqtam ītamar “he met a loss”
glossary.ana: to, for · with an infinitive, “to, for” (ana kirîm zaqāpim “to plant as an orchard”); “as” (ana kirîm), “into” (ana libbi), “at the rate of” (ana itêšu)
glossary.apālum: to answer; to satisfy, pay (a creditor): ippalma (present, with -ma) “he shall pay, and”
glossary.awīltum: woman, lady (feminine of awīlum; Harper awiltu): awīltam “woman” (accusative)
glossary.ašrum: place; ana ašrišu “to its (proper) place” · ašar “where”, with a verb in the subjunctive: ašar illiku “where he went”
glossary.bītum: house, estate · bīt karānim “wine-house, tavern” (construct form bīt, written É); bītiša “her house” (É-ša)
glossary.bīšum: movable property, goods, possessions: bīšašu “his goods”
glossary.dibtum: UNCERTAIN: credit, a loan on trust — Harper’s diptu “credit(?)”, with his own question mark: ana dibtim “on credit”
glossary.dâkum: to kill; N-stem iddâk “he shall be killed” — the code’s death sentence
glossary.ebūrum: harvest, the crop: ebūrim “of harvest, at harvest” (one logogram, read BURU₁₄; Harper writes ebûrim)
glossary.egûm: to be careless, neglect (Harper: “to be careless”): itēgi(ma) “he has been negligent, and”
glossary.ekallum: palace (É.GAL “great house”) — the crown as owner
glossary.erēbum: to enter: iterub “she has entered” (perfect; Harper I,2)
glossary.gagûm: UNCERTAIN: the cloister, the walled house in which the priestesses of the law lived (written MAL.GE.A, with the sign GE as GI₄ on the plate; Harper leaves the signs unread): ina gagîm “in the cloister”
glossary.ilum: god; here: the temple as owner · plural ilāni “gods” (written DINGIR.DINGIR, as in the litany): maḫar ilāni “before the gods”
glossary.ina: in, from · at (ina ebūrim “at harvest”); out of (ina bilat kirîm “out of the orchard’s yield”)
glossary.kanīkum: sealed receipt, sealed tablet (from kanākum “to seal”): kanīk kaspim “a sealed receipt for silver”, kanīkim (genitive); not the same word as kunukkum “seal”
glossary.karānum: wine (written GEŠ.TIN.NA; Harper karânu): bīt karānim “wine-house, tavern” (É + GEŠ.TIN.NA)
glossary.kaspum: silver — the code’s money, written KÙ.BABBAR “shining precious-metal” · kaspim: mišil mana kaspim “half a mina of silver” · with a spelled vowel after the logogram: KÙ.BABBAR-a-am, -i-im, -u-um: kaspam, kaspim, kaspum (accusative, genitive, nominative); kaspum as the subject; the grain-and-silver pair šeʾam u kaspam “grain and silver”
glossary.kânum-D: D-stem of kânum: to convict, prove against someone (uktīn, ukannūšuma)
glossary.leqûm: to take: ileqqi “he shall take” · ilqi “he took” (il-qi₂), ilqû (subjunctive, il-qu₂-u₂), ilqēma (il-qi₂-e-ma) “he took, and”, ilteqēma (perfect, il-te-qi₂-ma) “he has taken, and”; ša … ilqû “which he took” · ilqēma (il-qi₂-ma) “he took, and” (preterite ilqe + -ma, here without a spelled e); ilteqe (il-te-qi₂, perfect) “he has taken”; ileqqi (i-li-qi₂, present) “he shall take”; leqîm (li-qi₂-im, infinitive, genitive): ina kaspim leqîm “in the taking of the silver”
glossary.lā: not (in subordinate and nominal contexts) · before a noun in the genitive, “without”: lā kanīkim “without a sealed receipt”; in a šumma-clause, “not”: lā ītamar “he did not see”
glossary.lū: or; either (lū … lū “whether … or”); with verb: “let …”
glossary.mala: as many as, as much as (introducing a relative clause): mala ina kirîm ibbaššû “as many as are in the orchard”
glossary.manûm-count: to count, reckon (the verb; the noun manûm “mina” is another word): imannû(ma) “they shall count” — 3rd plural, impersonal
glossary.maḫar: before, in the presence of: maḫar ilim “before the god”
glossary.maḫārum: to receive: imḫur(u) · imḫur, imḫuru “he received” (preterite; subjunctive in a clause), imaḫḫar “he shall receive” (present); …ḫari… in a broken form · to face, withstand (litany): qabal lā maḫārim “combat none can face” · imtaḫar (im-ta-ḫar) “she received” (perfect; Harper’s maḫāru I,2, “to receive”): grain and silver for beer
glossary.maḫīrum: market rate, price: ana maḫīrātišunu “at their rates” · maḫīr šikarim “the rate of beer” (maḫīr, construct form, written KI.LAM; Harper maḫiru)
glossary.maṭûm-D: D-stem of maṭûm “to be little”: to reduce, diminish: umtaṭṭi (perfect) “he has reduced”
glossary.nadûm: to cast, throw (a charge; a body into the river): iddi, nadû, iddû · also to leave lying (a field): ittadi “he has left (it) lying” · of a flock: ṣēnī ana eqlim iddi “he turned the sheep loose into a field” · inaddûši (i-na-[ad]-du-u-ši) “they shall throw her” (present, plural, with -ši): ana mê inaddûši “they shall throw her into the water”
glossary.nadûm-Š: Š-stem of nadûm “to throw”: to make (someone) throw down, to strip of: uštaddišu (perfect, with -šu) “he made him throw (it) down”
glossary.nadānum: to give, pay: inaddin, iddinam, iddinušum; nadānim “to give” · iddin “he gave”; ana kaspim nadānum “to sell”: inaddinūma (present, plural) “they shall sell, and …” · iddin, iddinu “he gave” (preterite; the subjunctive -u in a ša- or inūma clause); iddinma “he gave, and”; …in, …din in broken forms; inaddin “he shall give”: ana damqaršu inaddin “he shall give to his merchant” · ittadinma (it-ta-di-in-ma) “he has given, and” (perfect); inaddinu (i-na-ad-di-nu) “(which) he gives” (present, with the subjunctive -u)
glossary.nakārum: UNCERTAIN: perhaps nakārum “to be hostile, to deny, to dispute”: only the first sign ik survives, which the editor doubts, so the form (ikkir-ma ?) and the sense are a guess; the verb is the editors’ restoration · ittakir (it-ta-ki-ir, perfect) “he denied, disowned (his merchant)”, ittakiršu “he denied him”, ikkiru (ik-ki-ru, preterite with the subjunctive -u) “(because) he denied”: here the forms are spelled out on the stele, so the verb nakārum is sure; Harper’s heading is “to be different, to be hostile, to dispute”
glossary.našûm: to bear, carry: ittanašši “he shall bear (the penalty)” · našû (na-šu-u, stative with the subjunctive -u) “(that) he carried”: mimma ša našû “anything that he carried”
glossary.nikkazzum: UNCERTAIN: account, credit (Harper nikkazzu; modern editions normalise nikkassum “account, reckoning”): ana nikkazzim “to the account”, spelled ni-ik-ka-az-zi-im; the sense “account” or “credit” is not secure
glossary.nīšum: oath (literally “life”): nīš ilim “the oath by the god”
glossary.pašārum: UNCERTAIN: the verb pašārum “to loosen, release”; in the merchant’s law, perhaps “to sell off, dispose of” (ana pašārim, restored by the editors as “for selling”): only pa-ša… survives, so the form and sense are a guess · ana pašārim (a-na pa-ša-ri-im) “for trading” — Harper’s glossary pašāru I,1 “to trade”: the stele spells the word out, so the form is sure; the sense is Harper’s reading (the editors’ restored “for selling” above was a guess)
glossary.petûm: to open; of land, to bring into cultivation: iptete “he has opened” · preterite ipte, iptēma “he opened”
glossary.qalûm: to burn (Harper qalû): iqallû(ši) “they shall burn (her)”
glossary.qaqqadum: head; the capital, the principal of a loan, as against its interest (written SAG.DU, “head”): ana qaqqadim “to the capital” (genitive, written with the logogram) · qaqqad kaspim “the capital of the silver” (construct form, here spelled ga-ga-ad)
glossary.qiāpum: to entrust, give in trust (Harper “to intrust”, listed under qâpu): iqīp(ma) “he entrusted (the agent), and”
glossary.rabûm: great; D/Š-stems “make great”; rabûtim “great (pl.)” · rabîtim (ra-bi-tim, feminine genitive) “large”: ina abnim rabîtim “by the large stone”
glossary.rakāsum-N: N-stem of rakāsum “to bind”: to gather, band together, conspire (Harper “collect”): ittarkasū(ma) “they have gathered, and”
glossary.redûm-lead: to lead, drive, bring (the verb; rēdûm “soldier” is another word; Harper “to conduct”): irdiam “she led (them) here”, with the ventive -am
glossary.sadārum: to set in a row, put in order; of an account, to write out, list: isaddar(ma) “he shall write out”. Harper files the same forms under šaṭāru “to write”; the reading sadārum rests on the plate sign SA (not ŠA) in i-sa-ad-dar-ma
glossary.sābītum: UNCERTAIN: the tavern-keeper, the woman who brews and sells beer (written ŠAL.GEŠ.TIN.NA, “woman” + “wine”); the reading sābītum follows the modern editors — Harper gives only the signs
glossary.tadmiqtum: a favour, a kindness (from damāqum “to be good”; Harper tadmiqtu “favor”): ana tadmiqtim “as a favour”; the commercial sense, an advance made on trust, is a guess from the context
glossary.tamkārum: merchant (written tam-KAR §32, DAM.GÀR §40): the ransom-fronting, land-buying businessman of the code · written dam-qar, dam-qar-um (the common syllabic spelling of the merchant): damqar, damqarum “the merchant” (nominative), damqaršu “his merchant” · written DAM.GÀR as a Sumerogram (Harper tamkaru [DAM-GAR]; two signs on the plate): tamkārum, tamkāram, tamkārim, tamkāršu
glossary.târum-D: D-stem of târum: to give back: turru “taken away/captured”; utarrūšumma “they shall return (it) to him” · utâr (present) “he shall hand back” · turrim (infinitive, tu-ur-ri-im): ana turrim “for repaying, to give back”; utâr (present) “he shall hand back” · uttēr (ut-te-ir, perfect) “he has given back”: the same verb as utâr
glossary.ugbabtum: UNCERTAIN: a priestess, written ŠAL.NIN.AN (Harper aššatum NIN.AN; NIN.AN is later written NIN.DINGIR, “lady of the god”); Harper gives no reading and translates only “a priestess”, later editions read ugbabtum, and the ŠAL may be only the woman-sign. The reading rests on the sign group and the context, not on a spelled word
glossary.usakani: UNCERTAIN: a kind of beer, written U.SA.KA.NI (four signs Harper leaves unread; no meaning known): šikarim usakani “beer of the usakani (kind?)”
glossary.wašābum: to sit: ul uššab “he shall not sit” (the stone writes uš-ta-ab — a carver’s slip Harper flags) · to dwell: wāšbum (participle, contracted) “the dweller, the tenant” (a conjectured reading, aš-bu-u[m]); wa… “dwell-” in broken forms · stative wašbat (wa-aš-ba-at) “she dwells, lives”: ša ina gagîm lā wašbat “who does not live in the cloister”
glossary.wašārum: D-stem (w)uššurum “to release, set free”: ūtaššar “he shall be released” · the form ūtaššar (ū-ta-aš-šar) is the Dt, the t-form of the D-stem, in the present: “he shall be released”; the “D-stem” named above is the stem family, and this form is its t-form (Dt)
glossary.zakārum: to name, declare: izzakar “he named”, izakkarma “he shall declare, and”
glossary.šakānum: to set, place: išakkanūšumma “they shall set for him (a term), and” · išakkanūšum (present, plural, dative -šum) “they shall place (it) for him”, i.e. count it to him · iššakkan (iš-ša-ak-ka-an, N-stem present) “it shall be put”: ul iššakkan “it shall not be put (in the account)”
glossary.šamallûm: UNCERTAIN: the merchant’s agent, his trading assistant: šamallim (genitive, ša-ma-al-li-im), šamallû (nominative, ša-ma-al-lu-u₂); the editors print a logogram with a complement, so the syllabic spellings are a placeholder · on the stele the word is the Sumerogram ŠÀ.GAN₂.LÁ (Harper SA.GAN.LAL; modern ŠAMAN₂.LÁ), the first two signs one fused group on the plate, so the meaning “agent” is sure and the syllabic spellings above were a placeholder; the case is read from the sentence (šamallûm, šamallâm, šamallîm), also with -šu: šamallīšu “his agent”
glossary.šamnum: oil, fat (written Ì.GIŠ, the signs NI + GIŠ): šamnam (accusative; Harper šamnu)
glossary.šanûm-Š: UNCERTAIN: šanûm “to repeat, do a second time”, so perhaps “to double”; uštašannâ (uš-ta-ša-an-na-ma, with -ma “and”) is a Š-stem perfect (ušta- is the perfect prefix) and is read as “he shall double (it)”, but the exact stem and the form are not secure; the sense follows the penalty of the law · on the stele (§101): uštašannâma (uš-ta-ša-na-ma, with -ma “and”) “he shall double (it)”, which Harper’s glossary lists as a Š-stem perfect of šanû “to duplicate, to double”; the form is as Harper has it and the exact stem is not secure
glossary.šeʾum: barley, grain (the ŠE sign) · ŠE-am, ŠE-im, ŠE-um, written with the logogram and a spelled vowel; šeʾum as the subject; ŠE-am-ma “grain only” (with the restricting -ma); in broken forms še…
glossary.šikarum: beer (written KAŠ; Harper šikaru): šikarim (genitive), also as the price or rate “of beer”
glossary.šipātum: wool (written SIG, as Harper’s glossary gives it): šipâtam (accusative; Harper šipâtu)
glossary.šumma: if — the word that opens every law of the code
glossary.šunūti: them (masculine plural, accusative): ṣarrūtim šunūti “those criminals”
glossary.šuāti: that, the aforesaid · as the independent pronoun “him”: šuāti u bīšašu “him and his goods”
glossary.šī: she, that (feminine pronoun, as the independent word): ŠAL.GEŠ.TIN.NA šī “that tavern-keeper”; the masculine is šū
glossary.ūmum: day; ūmišu “daily” (written UD-mi-šu) · plural “days”: ūmī (written UD-mi-) “days”: ina ūmīšu lā malûtim “in his days not full” (the days of a lease) · ūm “day” (UD), before a following word, in ūm NER lā “a day (when ?) NER not …” · ūmīšu (UD-mi-šu) “his days”: ūmīšu imannûma “they shall count his days”
glossary.ḫarrānum: road; campaign: ḫarrān šarrim “the king’s campaign” (spelled ḫar-ra-an, or carved with the road-sign KASKAL) · journey, the merchant’s trading trip: ana ḫarrānim “on a journey” (the editors print ḫarranim; the spelling ḫar-ra-nim is uncertain here), ina ḫarrānim “on the journey”
glossary.ṣabātum: to seize: iṣṣabat, ṣabtu · stative with the subjunctive -u: adi kirâm ṣabtu “as long as he holds the orchard” (with Harper’s kirûm: “as long as the orchard is held”) · iṣṣabtamma (iṣ-ṣa-ab-tam-ma) “she seized (them), and” (perfect with the ventive -am and -ma): lā iṣṣabtamma “and she did not seize”
glossary.ṣarrūtum: criminals, rogues, rebels (Harper: “outlaws, rowdies, traitors”): ṣarrūtum, ṣarrūtim (plural noun, not a title)
glossary.ṣibtum: interest (“increase”): ṣibtam; ṣibassu, ṣibtišu “its interest” · also written MÁŠ (the logogram, “increase”) and ṣib-tam; plural ṣibātim (ṣi-ba-tim) “interest(s)”; ṣibtim genitive · ṣibāt kaspim “the interest on the silver” (ṣibāt, construct form of the plural)
